title: The UK Is Failing Our On-the-Job Learners
author: Educating Hat Beasts
summary: The author interviews home-educating parent Nicola Leyland about the UK's GCSE resit system, arguing that England's insistence on passing GCSE English and maths before students can progress in vocational Level 3 qualifications traps talented, often neurodivergent, practical learners in a cycle of repeated failure. Roughly a third of students fail to reach a grade 4 each year, and only about 17 percent of resitters ever pass, yet colleges are financially incentivized to keep cycling students through retakes rather than let them advance in the trade or vocational subject where they excel. The piece uses the case of Leyland's autistic, dyslexic daughter Heidi, who thrives in personal training and youth work but has failed her English GCSE three times, to show how a 'spiky profile' of uneven cognitive strengths gets punished by a one-size-fits-all gatekeeping requirement. It closes by evaluating new UK government reforms, arguing that adding another tier of Level 1 stepping-stone qualifications does not remove the underlying maths-and-English gate, so the reform is unlikely to fix what it claims to address.
points: The core policy failure identified is structural, not motivational: only about 17% of GCSE English/maths resitters ever pass, yet colleges are financially penalized for not enrolling non-passers in retakes, creating an 'endless nightmare' loop rather than a path forward.

The 'spiky profile' framing reframes neurodivergent and dyslexic students' struggles as an inability to learn certain subjects in that format at all, not a motivation or effort problem, challenging the assumption that more resits will eventually produce a pass.

Government reform (new Level 1 stepping-stone qualifications) is shown to preserve rather than remove the maths-and-English gate to Level 3 vocational progression, meaning the same students will still be blocked from their chosen trade.

Real-world case evidence (a student blocked from nursing training despite passing a health and social care qualification, a hairdressing student diverted to barbering) illustrates how the gate diverts students away from their actual talents and career paths.
quotes: Around a third of GCSE students get less than a 4 (what used to be a 'D') every year. Supporters point out that everyone could get a 4, in theory, as students are graded on a curve against historic data, but there's no suggestion of lowering the standard or anything else that leads to grade inflation.

But, the reality is only around 17% of resitters ever pass and, as colleges are allegedly refused funds for students not taking resits (the government disagrees), young people wind up in an endless nightmare of failing again and again and again.

Yet, some of these young people are among our most talented practical learners - the tradies and crafters of tomorrow. Some are neurodivergent, with brains that excel in specialisation - good at maths or language, but not both.

There's maybe 10 or 20% of kids across a classroom who are 'spiky' - they are clever, they can get an A grade in one subject, but a D grade in another, and by insisting maths and English are more important than anything else, you're creating a massive problem.

There's only 17% who pass these retakes. They go onto do Level 3 in their chosen subject. The rest are sent back to do a Level 2 in a different subject, which isn't their chosen skill, their passion - they're being diverted.
People will never get jobs if you insist on this 'lid' of maths and English GCSE or else they can't train vocationally. You're creating a system that literally holds people back.
When you judge people wholly on their deficits and put them on the scrap heap so young, how is our country going to succeed?
